declarations.documentation:
The SHA-256 digest of @text@'s UTF-8 bytes, as 64 lowercase hex characters. Deterministic and pure,
so a replay recomputes the same digest. Typical uses: a content dedupe key, or a stable tag for an
external identifier — but note that a plain digest of an ENUMERABLE input (a numeric user id, an
email) is reversible by dictionary: anyone can hash every candidate and match. For a tag that must
not be reversible, use `hmac_sha256` with a secret key. Takes PUBLIC text only — hashing a secret
would raise a declassification question (is the digest of a secret still secret?) that this plain
digest deliberately leaves unanswered; `hmac_sha256` answers it for the keyed form.
declarations.name: sha256

parameters.documentation: The text to digest, hashed as its UTF-8 bytes.
parameters.label: text

text.description: The text to digest, hashed as its UTF-8 bytes.

declarations.signature: primitive agent sha256(text: string) -> string

declarations.documentation:
The HMAC-SHA-256 tag of @text@ under the secret @key@, as 64 lowercase hex characters — the
IRREVERSIBLE tag `sha256` cannot give over an enumerable input: without the key a dictionary attack
is impossible, so hashing a user id with a secret key yields a pseudonym that is stable for one key
and opaque to everyone without it (a chat bot's abuse-attribution tag is the canonical use; rotating
the key rotates every pseudonym). The result is deliberately PUBLIC despite the private key: an HMAC
tag reveals nothing about the key by construction — irreversibility IS the sound declassification —
so this is the one prim whose result the runtime does not taint private. Deterministic, so a replay
recomputes the same tag.
declarations.name: hmac_sha256

parameters.documentation: The text to tag, as its UTF-8 bytes; public, like `sha256`'s.
parameters.label: text

Perform an HTTP request to @url@ with @method@, the given @headers@ and @body@ — EXACTLY `fetch`'s
request — but capture the RESPONSE body as a downloaded `file` rather than as text. The bytes land in the
blob store and the reply carries only the slim @file@ HANDLE; the raw bytes (and their base64) never touch
the value plane, the durable call record, or the trace. This is the receive-side twin of a `binary`
REQUEST body, and it exists for the same reason: to keep a payload's bytes OFF the value plane. A plain
`fetch` of a megabyte image would read it into the response `body` STRING, dragging that text (and its
base64, once re-encoded) through every value, event, and trace it flows into — whereas `fetch_file` streams
it straight to a blob and hands back a handle. Reach for it to download a file by URL: an image, a PDF, a
CSV export, a release artifact. It is NOT for a base64 field buried inside a JSON reply (a data-URI in an
API's JSON document) — `fetch_file` only ever captures the WHOLE response body; decode an embedded base64
string with `files.from_base64` after an ordinary `fetch`. The downloaded @file@'s recorded content type is
the response's `Content-Type` (falling back to `application/octet-stream` when the server sent none).
Returns the response @status@ code (branch on it exactly like `fetch` — a non-2xx reply's body is still
captured to a @file@, so a caller inspects @status@ before trusting the download), its @headers@ (names
lowercased; repeated headers joined with ", "), and the downloaded @file@. A request that never completes
throws `fetch_error`, exactly like `fetch`.

An authenticated API call was rejected over WHO IS CALLING: the endpoint answered @status@ — 401 or
403 — so the CREDENTIAL is what failed: revoked, expired past what its holder believed, or scoped too
narrowly for this call. Retrying with the SAME credential cannot succeed; the recovery is a fresh
RESOLUTION of it, which is why the ordinary composition is a `supervise` converter that signals
`supervise.interrupted`: the re-run resolves the credential again, and one the runtime cannot refresh parks
the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation — a human's re-authorization prompt — rather than
failing. That is the whole line this variant draws: an `auth_error` may need a HUMAN before any retry can
work, an `api_error` never does.

(403 is read as auth even though some APIs also spend it on quota exhaustion. The access-rejection reading
is the one worth composing a re-resolution around, and a quota 403 that is replayed simply fails again.)

@context@ says WHICH call failed in the caller's own words, and @message@ carries the server's own body —
the two halves a human needs, kept apart so a renderer can show either without splitting a string.

401/403 — a malformed request, a resource that is not there, a rate limit, a server error. Nothing about

policy downstream reads a number, never a message.

verbatim, because it is the diagnosis and a model handed this error reads it and adjusts.

declarations.documentation:
Classify a non-2xx @status@ into the shared vocabulary: 401 and 403 are `auth_error` (a credential
problem no retry with the same credential can fix), EVERY other status is `api_error`. @context@ and
@message@ ride onto whichever variant comes out, unchanged.

This is the ONE place the line is drawn, and that is the point. The classification used to be re-decided
per package — `gmail`, `google_calendar`, `tavily` and every OAuth REST integration written after them each
carried a private copy of the same two-arm `match`, so "Google's 401" and "Anthropic's 401" wore
different types and an app composing two of them wrote one `supervise` converter per package to say the same
thing twice. With one classifier the vocabulary is one vocabulary: a converter matches `http.auth_error`
once and covers every API behind it.

The STATUS IS RETAINED on the way out, deliberately. A caller downstream decides whether to back off and
repeat (408 / 429 / 5xx) or to give up (a 400 the service is refusing), and that decision is a number
comparison on `api_error.status` — never a substring search through a human sentence, which is what the
statusless vocabulary forced. Reach for this at the ONE boundary where a package reads its responses; it
answers a VALUE, so the caller chooses whether to throw it, fold it, or attach it to an outcome.
declarations.name: classify_status

anyOf.description:
api_error: An authenticated API call failed for anything OTHER than the credential: a non-2xx @status@ that is not
401/403 — a malformed request, a resource that is not there, a rate limit, a server error. Nothing about
the caller's identity is in question, so backing off and replaying the call AS IT STANDS is the whole
recovery for the transient half, and the other half (a 400 the service is simply refusing) will keep
failing until the ARGUMENT changes.

WHICH half a given failure is, is read off @status@ and nowhere else: 408 / 429 / 5xx are the transient
ones a retry policy should back off and repeat, every other status is a refusal that will repeat forever.
That is the whole reason the status RIDES on the error instead of being folded into a sentence — a retry
policy downstream reads a number, never a message.

@context@ says WHICH call failed in the caller's own words; @message@ carries the server's own body
verbatim, because it is the diagnosis and a model handed this error reads it and adjusts.

$katari_constructor.description: The tag that selects this variant. Write this exact string.

anyOf.description:
auth_error: An authenticated API call was rejected over WHO IS CALLING: the endpoint answered @status@ — 401 or
403 — so the CREDENTIAL is what failed: revoked, expired past what its holder believed, or scoped too
narrowly for this call. Retrying with the SAME credential cannot succeed; the recovery is a fresh
RESOLUTION of it, which is why the ordinary composition is a `supervise` converter that signals
`supervise.interrupted`: the re-run resolves the credential again, and one the runtime cannot refresh parks
the run on a `prelude.oauth.authorize` escalation — a human's re-authorization prompt — rather than
failing. That is the whole line this variant draws: an `auth_error` may need a HUMAN before any retry can
work, an `api_error` never does.

(403 is read as auth even though some APIs also spend it on quota exhaustion. The access-rejection reading
is the one worth composing a re-resolution around, and a quota 403 that is replayed simply fails again.)

@context@ says WHICH call failed in the caller's own words, and @message@ carries the server's own body —
the two halves a human needs, kept apart so a renderer can show either without splitting a string.

(`text(target = field(target = ..., key = ...))`) is what a document walker actually writes at nearly every

declarations.documentation:
Plug an MCP server's tools into a program for the extent of @continuation@, as a scoped provider —
the `use mcp.provide(url = ..., auth = ...)` form. The runtime lists the server (a missing or dead
`oauth` credential pauses on an authorization escalation and retries once answered; rejected `headers`
material throws `auth_error`; a rejected listing throws `server_error`), hands @continuation@
a `toolbox[Scope]` of one runtime-minted agent per tool (each carrying the server signature — for
`reflection.get_metadata` and call-site validation — and the descriptor it was listed with), and settles
with the continuation's result. `Scope` rides the continuation's row (that is what a tool call raises) and
is DISCHARGED from `provide`'s own row, so a tool cannot escape the block: the scope closes when
@continuation@ returns (or the run is cancelled), and a stray later call is rejected as a typed
`server_error`. `Scope` is the marker the tools are gated by — the built-in `mcp.scope` for the dynamic
path, or a generated binding's module-local marker; pass it explicitly as the first `[...]` argument
(`mcp.provide[mcp.scope](...)`), and the toolbox binder's annotation must agree. Discharging `Scope` is
`provide`'s alone (only it opens the connection), so a live tool context cannot be forged. @url@ is a plain
routing value: the runtime connects and caches under the `{url, auth}` descriptor.
DECLARE ONE MARKER PER LOGICAL CONNECTION. When you call `provide` directly you choose `Scope` yourself:
share ONE marker across two connections and their scopes MERGE at the type level (the two servers' tools
become mutually substitutable in a row that carries the marker) — the same widening the old dynamic-URL
`toolbox[string]` had, no worse. It is only a TYPE distinction: routing and the live-`provide` backstop are
always enforced by each tool value's own `{url, auth}` descriptor, so a call never reaches the wrong
server — at worst a tool whose `provide` has closed fails with a typed `server_error`. A `katari mcp pull`
binding needs no such discipline: its module namespace mints a distinct marker (`github.connection`) per
connection automatically, so pulled servers never share a scope. When the toolbox itself is never read —
a pulled binding's tools call through the static `mcp.call` — `open` is the listing-free form of this
same contract.

data-driven form of `provide`. The marker is minted once, UNCONDITIONALLY, whatever the array holds:
an optional connection is an `if` in the DATA (append it to the array or not), never a branch around
the `use`, so conditional connections stop forking the program's shape (the 2×2 explosion). The
continuation receives one toolbox per connection, in input order — flatten what you hand an AI loop
(`array.map` + `record.values` + `array.flatten`). Connections open one by one in order and tear
down in reverse; any connection's listing failure is the same typed error a lone `provide` raises,
and tears the already-open ones down. An empty array runs @continuation@ with no toolboxes — the
same row shape, so callers never branch on emptiness. This must be an external, not a composition:
only the runtime actually opening the scope can discharge the marker (a plain agent composing
`provide`s could not type the empty set — there would be nothing to discharge a never-minted
marker).

Call one tool on an MCP server directly — the static counterpart of `provide`, with no listing and no
minted agent value. The seam the binding modules `katari mcp pull` generates are built on: @tool@ is the
server-declared tool name, @arguments@ its arguments object as a plain value tree (records / arrays /
scalars, and a `file` becomes base64 in place — the same slot contract as `http.json`). The result is
read as a value and checked against @T@ inside the runtime: a `$katari_ref` handle object becomes a REAL
`file` value, records / arrays / scalars land as themselves, a plain-text reply reads only into a
string-shaped @T@, and a mismatch throws `validation_error`. Instantiate @T@ with `unknown` to keep the

tainted secret and may flow only to a submission sink — an http `Authorization` header — never to a
user-facing boundary). The runtime holds the token material and refreshes it on demand, so no token ever

while the RECORDED expiry holds (with a ~60s refresh margin), refreshing once due; the runtime owns the
caching, so a program that keeps its own copy only defeats the refresh. The flip side, which callers must
design around: because the stored expiry is the only input, a token revoked BEFORE it expires keeps being
served, and the API answers 401 / 403 for up to one access-token lifetime. Convert that downstream failure
into a `supervise.interrupted` to recover automatically — see this module's header.

an instant ("mail that arrived after T"). The cursor is the floor; it advances to each delivered
item's own @mark@, never past the tick that observed it, and never on the poller's clock. The memory
alongside it is only the keys at or above the floor, so it stays CONSTANT-SIZE forever: a key below
the floor has nothing left to prevent, because an item that far back can no longer be listed.

does not document whether it means `>` or `>=`, so `overlap = 1000` makes both readings safe). The
overlap costs no duplicates — the keys inside it are exactly the ones still remembered — and an
@overlap@ of 0 is right for a source whose listing boundary is exact.

declarations.documentation:
Dedup by a BOUNDED SET OF KEYS — for a source with no usable receive clock, only a window that
slides ("meetings starting within the next 30 minutes"). No cursor moves; every fetch sees the same
`since` and works from the tick instant instead. The memory is the most recent @capacity@ keys.

RE-NOTIFY HAZARD IT LEAVES: forgetting the oldest key means an item that is STILL inside the window
after @capacity@ other items have been delivered will be delivered again. Size @capacity@ well above
the largest number of items one window can hold (google_calendar uses 200 for a 30-minute lead) and
the drop only ever reaches keys long past; size it too small and a busy window re-notifies its own
head. There is no cheaper bound — the memory has to forget something, and age is the only safe axis.

list from, so whatever crossed the window while the subscription was down is simply gone. `resume`
still earns its keep here — it stops the re-notification storm a re-primed memory would cause — but
only a `watermark` subscription delivers its downtime.

declarations.documentation:
Poll a source on @schedule@ and deliver each item it has not seen before to @deliver_to@, forever —
the durable-subscription skeleton every source package composes instead of rewriting. Shaped like
`time.watch` (`-> never`, @deliver_to@'s effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged), so it
composes under `parallel [ … ]` beside any other daemon and beside other subscriptions.

DELIVERY IS AT-LEAST-ONCE. An item reaches @deliver_to@ one or more times, never zero: the commit lands
only after a delivery returns, so a crash or a throw in between re-delivers exactly that item on the
next tick. Build exactly-once at the DESTINATION by making the delivery idempotent — keyed by
`item.key`, which is the identity this loop already promises is stable.

WHAT @fetch@ MUST GUARANTEE, and it is the whole adapter: given @since@ (the instant this tick lists
from — the cursor's floor minus the regime's overlap) and @tick@ (the occurrence's scheduled instant),
return every item at or above @since@, OLDEST FIRST, across every page of the source's pagination.
Oldest-first is load-bearing: the cursor then only ever passes items that have actually been
delivered, so a delivery that throws mid-tick leaves the rest of the tick still above the cursor.
Draining every page is load-bearing too: a listing cut off at a cap that orders newest-first hands
back only the newest matches, and a cursor advanced over them strands the older ones below it forever.
Returning an item AGAIN that was returned before is free — that is what the remembered keys are for.

WHAT IT REPORTS. With `skip_backlog` it reports ARRIVALS: whatever the source already held when the
subscription first started is never delivered, however well it matches, and an old item that comes to
match LATER is not delivered either (the fetch never looks below the cursor). That is the right shape
for hearing about new things and the wrong one for "tell me whenever anything matches"; a listing
agent answers the latter.

RESTARTS. With `continuity = resume(key = ...)` the cursor lives in the store, so a runtime restart, a
re-forked fiber and a `supervise` re-run all RESUME from it — and the items that arrived while the
subscription was down are delivered, oldest first, on the tick after it comes back. With `fresh()`
every activation re-primes and that downtime is skipped for good. Nothing else about the subscription
changes between the two.

NO RETRY IS BUILT IN — a failing @fetch@ or @deliver_to@ propagates and kills the subscription, exactly
as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Compose resilience at the call site: `supervise.forever` plus a
converter that turns the transient failures (and, for an OAuth source, `auth_error`) into
`supervise.interrupted`. With `resume`, the backoff costs nothing but latency; the cursor survives it.

The first poll is one @schedule@ occurrence in (a `time.watch` occurrence fires one interval AFTER the
start), and under `seen_set` + `skip_backlog` that first poll is the priming one — so the earliest
notification such a subscription can produce is two occurrences after it starts.

Pin `Scope` and the ceiling `E` as the first two type arguments (`region.provide[region.scope, my_effects]`); `R` and the residual outer row are inferred from the continuation. Discharging `Scope` is `provide`'s alone (only it opens the nursery), so a live nursery context cannot be forged. NEST UNDER DISTINCT MARKERS: share one marker across two nurseries and their scopes MERGE (fibers become mutually cancellable), so declare a module-local `effect` per nursery when nesting.

declarations.documentation: Spawn @task@ (applied to @argument@) as a fiber in the nursery @nursery@, returning immediately with a `fiber[Scope]` handle (identity only — for `cancel`; read its runtime-minted id with `fiber_id`). @name@ is an optional opaque tag the runtime echoes back wherever it talks about this fiber (`roster`, `crashed`, `failed`) — give one to any fiber something might later need to name. @task@ is `-> null`: A FIBER CARRIES NO RESULT. Everything a fiber produces leaves through its ESCALATIONS (surfacing at `watch`) — a task with something to deliver performs a request carrying it as its LAST act, and what the task returns is discarded when it settles. The type makes the discipline total: a `-> T` task does not fit, so a result cannot be silently dropped — it must have been delivered (or deliberately not produced) before the task can end. (`-> never` bodies — a watcher that runs until cancelled — fit by subtyping.) @task@'s effect must fit under the ceiling `E` (a child that raises less is fine; one that raises more is a type error) — EXCEPT ITS THROWS: the task parameter's row is `E | prelude.throw[unknown]`, so a throwing task forks under a throw-free ceiling. That is not a loophole but the boundary's contract made type: an uncaught throw never crosses the region AS a throw (it is trapped at `watch` and delivered as the typed `failed` event), so the ceiling — what `watch` actually re-emits — stays free of `prelude.throw`, and every fiber is bounded by `E` plus the two ending events, which is exactly what makes `watch` a total obligation. The fiber's escalations do not surface here; they well up at `watch`. A FIBER'S UNCAUGHT THROW NEEDS NO GUARD AND NO CEILING ENTRY: catch inside the task what the task can genuinely answer, and leave the rest to `failed`. Scope-gated (`with Scope`): callable only inside the `provide` that opened this nursery.

declarations.documentation: The nursery's WHITE HOLE: re-emit the fibers' escalations into the enclosing program as the ceiling effect `E`, plus the runtime's own `crashed` and `failed` events. It returns `never` — it only ever raises, never yields — so install a `handler` (or any row that covers `E | crashed | failed`) around it to service the fibers' requests. Because every fiber's effect fits under `E` and `watch` re-emits the FULL `E`, covering `E | crashed | failed` here covers everything any fiber can surface. This is the ONE channel out of a fiber: a normal completion is silent (the settled `null` is discarded — a task that has something to say says it as its last act), a `cancel` is silent (the canceller knows), and the TWO endings a task cannot report itself arrive as typed events — a PANIC as `crashed`, an uncaught `prelude.throw` as `failed`. In both the runtime tears the ended fiber down and reports the ending as data, so what a death MEANS is your handler's decision, not an unwinding accident; and because the throw is trapped HERE, no `fork` has to wrap its task in a throw guard just to keep the region standing. Scope-gated (`with Scope`): callable only inside the opening `provide`. A fiber may escalate BEFORE any `watch` is installed (it forks, then waits on an FFI / http / AI call, and the watch is set up only later): every such escalation is held DURABLY and re-emitted the moment a `watch` registers, in arrival order — so a watch installed arbitrarily late still receives every earlier escalation, and a fiber need not delay its first raise until a watch is up. WATCH IS TRANSPARENT — IT IMPOSES NO SERIALIZATION OF ITS OWN. It re-emits EVERY fiber escalation CONCURRENTLY, the moment it arrives, so the ONLY serialization point is the RECEIVING handler: a sequential (stateful `var`) handler serializes its OWN invocations at its FIFO, in ARRIVAL order, while a `parallel handler` runs them concurrently. So two escalations to DIFFERENT handlers are ALWAYS concurrent (a handler blocked on one — say a human-latency approval — never starves another), and two to the SAME var handler serialize at that handler in arrival order (a chat loop keeps ONE var handler and stays in order for free). ONE watch is enough: it interleaves every fiber's stream by construction — do NOT run several to gain concurrency (the concurrency is already there; the desks are told apart by their handlers, not by extra watches).

declarations.documentation:
A fiber FAILED — re-emitted at `watch` by the runtime in place of the fiber's uncaught
`prelude.throw`: the throw left the fiber's task with nothing inside it left to catch it, so the
runtime tears the fiber down and reports the thrown value as DATA instead of letting the throw
unwind your watch context. @error@ is the thrown value ITSELF, untouched, so a handler `match`es it
exactly as a `prelude.throw` handler would. Fire-and-forget (`-> null`): handle it above your

region down. It rides `watch`'s row, so handling it is part of the region's total obligation. THIS

the region, so a `fork`'s task row carries only the throws the task itself handles. NOT `crashed`:
a throw is a failure a CORRECT program meets and its payload is typed domain data, while a panic is
a defect in the program and carries only a message — same `(id, name, <reason>)` shape, different
question. Not meant to be performed by programs (the runtime is its one author); a program that

declarations.documentation:
Canonicalise @name@ into a store path SEGMENT, or `null` when it cannot be one: trimmed, lower-cased,
and then required to be non-empty and spelled only in lowercase letters, digits, `-` and `_`. ONE
offending character rejects the whole name — this is not a sanitiser, and deliberately so: silently
stripping a `/` out of "a/b" would hand back "ab", a DIFFERENT name than the one the caller asked
for, and two distinct requests would quietly land in one place.

The charset is what a KEY can hold without meaning something else. No `/` (that is a new segment), so no
`.` and therefore no `..` (that would climb out of the workspace a facility exists to confine), no
whitespace, and no case distinction — a store key compares byte-wise, so "Weight" and "weight" would
be two series a reader sees as one.

Reach for it wherever a name a MODEL or a USER supplied becomes part of a key (a worker's directory, a
metric series, a topic): the answer is the name to store under, and `null` is the app's cue to write its
own corrective sentence back to whoever proposed it. The trimming and lower-casing are part of the
answer, not a precondition — pass the raw text and store what comes back, so the same name typed twice
with different spacing or case is the same cell.

declarations.documentation:
Open the workspace at @path@ under the current one, for the extent of @continuation@ — the
`use store.scope(path = ...)` form, the store's `cd`. Four handlers catch the store operations and
RE-PERFORM them outward with the prefixed key (`get(key = "index")` under a scope at "core"
escalates as `get(key = "core/index")`; a `list` gets @path@ prepended to its own path
parameter), so nested scopes accumulate prefixes and the outermost bare perform is project-root
access — unhandled at the very top, the runtime machine-answers against the project's durable rows.
The handlers are PARALLEL on purpose: a scope is pure prefix arithmetic and must not serialize the
traffic passing through it (a turn's tool batch stays concurrent); ordering is `serialize`'s job,
never a workspace's. And a scope is a one-way descent: there is deliberately no `..`, so data
several workspaces share is NOT reached by path escape — it is reached by a REQUEST served ABOVE the
workspaces, whose clause opens the shared subtree's own scope in its body. That proxy is the
semantics: a request is what an inner install can never capture by accident. `share` / `shared`
below is that proxy, generalised once so it need not be respelt per shared cell.

@path@ is one or more `/`-separated SEGMENTS, each spelled as `safe_segment` requires (lowercase
letters, digits, `-`, `_`). A path that is not — an empty segment, a `..`, a stray space, a name a model
chose and nobody checked — PANICS here rather than opening a workspace somewhere else: the descent is
the program's own geometry, so a malformed one is a defect in the program and not an outcome a caller
could route. Validate a name that came from OUTSIDE the program with `safe_segment` first, and render
its `null` into whatever sentence the proposer should read.

ONE IMPRECISION TO KNOW ABOUT, because it shows up in the escalation report. All four clauses are
installed, and each re-performs its own operation, so this agent's row names all four whatever the
continuation actually does — a caller that only reads still carries `set` and `delete` outward. The row
is sound (a scope really can perform all four on its continuation's behalf) but it is coarser than the
truth, so the report reads as though a read-only agent could delete. Narrowing it needs the row to
follow which requests the continuation performs, which the language cannot express yet; until it can,
read a scoped agent's store row as "reaches the store" rather than as the set of operations it uses.
declarations.name: scope

declarations.documentation:
Run @task@ as a CRITICAL SECTION of the nearest enclosing `serialize`: the provider's SEQUENTIAL
handler calls it in its own body, so two exclusives of one domain can never interleave — the
handler's FIFO is the atomicity, even against a `parallel for` tool batch. The row is FIXED to the
store operations: a critical section reads, computes and writes, NOTHING ELSE — any other input is
computed BEFORE entering and closed over (as `modify` closes over its transform), so a section can
never block on a model, a network, or another domain. TWO GEOMETRY FACTS, both load-bearing: the
task runs AT THE SERIALIZE INSTALL SITE, not at this perform site — so a facility's subdirectory
prefix must be applied INSIDE the task body (`use store.scope(path = "memory")` as the task's
first move; a scope around the perform site does not travel with the task, but the install site's
own enclosing workspaces do apply). And an `exclusive` binds to the NEAREST enclosing `serialize`:
an inner domain shadows an outer one BY DESIGN — the nearest domain is the semantics, exactly as
the nearest workspace is. The task's answer crosses the handler as `unknown`; narrow it back with a
`match` (or `json.validate[T]`). A `serialize` (or `workspace`) in the program is the nearest domain;
with NONE installed above the perform, the RUNTIME serves it as the outermost domain — the task runs
at the PROJECT ROOT (project-root keys) in one durable, project-wide FIFO across every run. For a section
whose answer has a KNOWN shape, `exclusive_as[T]` below packages that narrowing.

declarations.documentation:

answer against T's schema and hand it back as a T. Everything `exclusive` says still holds — the row is

site, and it binds to the NEAREST enclosing `serialize`; the only difference is that the answer does not
cross back as `unknown`, so a caller stops respelling the same defensive `match` at every critical section.
T is read off @task@'s own declared result type, so it is normally inferred rather than written; it must be
a PUBLIC type, since a critical section's answer crosses `exclusive` as a public `unknown` and a secret
therefore never rides back out of one (read a secret from the store INSIDE the section instead). A
non-conforming answer throws `json.validation_error`, and that is NOT a condition to recover from: @task@
produced the value and its signature named the type, so a mismatch can only be the WRITER'S schema
mistake. Reach for the bare `exclusive` when the section's answer is genuinely shape-irregular.

declarations.documentation:
Open a serial domain for the extent of @continuation@ — the bare `use store.serialize` form (no
arguments, no type arguments: the domain is WHERE it is installed). Serves `exclusive` with a
deliberately SEQUENTIAL handler: its FIFO applies critical sections one at a time, in arrival
order, which is the whole point (a `parallel handler` would forfeit the atomicity). THE INSTALL
DISCIPLINE: a desk's dispatch clause installs its workspace and its domain together —
`use store.scope(path = <its workspace>)` then `use store.serialize` — once per dispatch. The race
this closes is exactly one turn's parallel tool batch, so a turn-lifetime FIFO covers it, and the
turns themselves already serialize at the desk's own sequential handler; tasks re-perform their
store operations from THIS install site, so installing under the workspace is what routes a
critical section's keys into it. An `exclusive` performed below a nested install binds to the
NEAREST domain (inner shadows outer, by design); one performed with no install above it rides to
the run root, where the RUNTIME serves it as the project-wide root domain — project-root keys, every
run's sections in ONE durable FIFO — so install a domain when a narrower extent is the semantics.

declarations.documentation:
Run @task@ AT THE NEAREST ENCLOSING `share`'s install site — that site's workspaces, that site's
serial domain — and hand back what it answered: the ONE request by which a desk reaches knowledge
living ABOVE its own workspace. The geometry is `exclusive`'s, and both halves are load-bearing. The
task is a CLOSURE that travels UP and runs THERE, so a workspace around this PERFORM does not travel
with it (the INSTALL site's own enclosing workspaces do apply) — which means a subdirectory of the
shared place is opened INSIDE the task body (`use store.scope(path = "shared/soul")` as its first
move), and that is exactly what lets one `share` serve every shared cell instead of one named request
per cell. And it binds to the NEAREST enclosing `share`: an inner shared place shadows an outer one BY
DESIGN, the same dynamic-scope rule the nearest workspace and the nearest serial domain follow. The
row is FIXED to the store operations plus `exclusive`: a task reads, computes and writes, and takes
ATOMICITY by wrapping a read-modify-write in `store.exclusive` INSIDE the task — which lands in the
shared place's own serial domain, since that is where the task is running. Nothing else is in the row,
so a shared access can never block on a model, a network or another domain. The answer crosses back as
`unknown`; narrow it with a `match` (or `json.validate[T]`), or reach for `shared_as[T]` below.
Unlike the store's four operations and `exclusive`, this one is NOT runtime-served, deliberately:
there is no project-root shared place, because a shared place is somewhere a program CHOSE and a
forgotten install must never quietly resolve to project-root keys. With no `share` above it a `shared`
rides to the run root as an ordinary unanswered request — the fate of any provider-backed request that
lost its provider — so the real guard is the effect row, which keeps `shared` visible in every
signature between the perform and the install.

against T's schema and hand it back as a T — what `exclusive_as` is to `exclusive`. Everything
`shared` says still holds: the row is FIXED to the store operations plus `exclusive`, the task runs AT
THE `share` INSTALL SITE rather than at this perform site, and it binds to the NEAREST enclosing
`share`; the only difference is that the answer does not cross back as `unknown`, so a reader of a
shared cell stops respelling the same defensive `match` at every access — which matters more here than
anywhere, since a shared cell is read from several desks and each would otherwise narrow it again. T is
read off @task@'s own declared result type, so it is normally inferred rather than written; it must be
a PUBLIC type, since the answer crosses `shared` as a public `unknown` and a secret therefore never
rides back out of the shared place (read a secret from the store INSIDE the task instead). A
non-conforming answer throws `json.validation_error`, and that is NOT a condition to recover from:
@task@ produced the value and its signature named the type, so a mismatch can only be the WRITER'S
schema mistake. Reach for the bare `shared` when the answer is genuinely shape-irregular.

declarations.documentation:
The TYPED shared CRITICAL SECTION: run @task@ in the shared place, as one `store.exclusive` of that
place's serial domain, and hand its answer back as a T — `shared_as` and `exclusive_as` in one call.

This exists because the two typed wrappers DO NOT COMPOSE, and the reason is structural rather than an
oversight. `shared_as[T]` reads T off a task that answers T; a task that wraps its body in
`store.exclusive` answers whatever `exclusive` answers, and `exclusive` is a REQUEST — its reply crosses
the handler boundary as `unknown`, which no inner `exclusive_as` can restore (the narrowing would have to
happen inside a task the outer wrapper cannot see the type of). So the read-modify-write of a shared cell
— the single most ordinary thing to do with one — fell out of both wrappers, and every site wrote a bare
`shared` around a bare `exclusive` plus a hand-written `json.validate`, each with its own paragraph
re-deriving why the helpers did not apply. This is that composition, spelled once.

Everything both wrappers say still holds. The task runs AT THE `share` INSTALL SITE (so a subdirectory of
the shared place is opened INSIDE the task body, `use store.scope(path = "shared/soul")` as its first
move), it binds to the NEAREST enclosing `share`, and inside it the section is atomic against every other
`exclusive` of that place's domain — which is the domain that matters here, since the shared place is
where the contention is. The row is FIXED to the four store operations: @task@ does not perform
`exclusive` itself (this agent wraps it), so it reads, computes and writes and nothing else.

T is read off @task@'s own declared result type and must be PUBLIC, for the same reason `shared_as`'s
must: the answer crosses two `unknown` request boundaries on the way out. A non-conforming answer throws
`json.validation_error` and is a WRITER's schema mistake, not a condition to recover from.
declarations.name: shared_exclusive_as

declarations.documentation:
Open the SHARED PLACE for the extent of @continuation@ — the bare `use store.share` form (no
arguments, no type arguments: the shared place is WHERE it is installed, exactly as a serial domain
is). Serves `shared` by calling its task in the clause body, so a task runs HERE — under this site's
workspaces, over this site's serial domain — while the desks below go on opening their own workspaces
per dispatch and reaching nothing of each other's. THE INSTALL DISCIPLINE, in this order: the app's
workspace, then `share`, then the desks (`use store.workspace(path = "assistant")` then
`use store.share`). The order is a CONTRACT, not a habit: a task's row carries `exclusive` and this
provider re-performs it outward, so `share` must sit INSIDE a serial domain for a shared critical
section to land in one — `workspace` (scope AND serialize in one install) above it is the ordinary way
to satisfy that. The order is legible in the TYPE, not only in prose: install `share` above the domain
instead and its `exclusive` finds nothing to catch it, so `store.exclusive` surfaces in the enclosing
signature and those sections ride to the runtime's project-wide root FIFO — legal, and visibly a
different program. The handler is PARALLEL on purpose: sending a closure upward is not an ordering
decision, and a sequential clause would queue three desks' concurrent reads of the shared place behind
one another for nothing; ordering is `exclusive`'s job here as everywhere, taken INSIDE the task. A
second `share` below this one captures every `shared` under it — the ordinary dynamic-scope rule, and
the way a deliberately NARROWER shared place (a sub-team's own commons, shared among its desks and
invisible to the app's) is expressed. KNOW WHAT THE GENERALISATION COSTS: a request per cell is also a
CAPABILITY per cell — a desk holding `read_digest` and not `save_digest_entry` cannot write the digest
whatever it does — and one `shared` is one capability over the WHOLE shared place. Where a boundary
BETWEEN shared cells is the semantics, keep the named request for that cell; the two compose, since a
named proxy installed below this one can perform `shared` in its own clause.

declarations.documentation:
Append @value@ to the bounded log at @key@ under @retention@, and answer what the bound did — the ONE
read-modify-write behind every "keep the newest N and say what fell off" series. The cell holds
`{ items, dropped }`; this reads it, applies the policy, writes it back, and returns `accepted(kept,
evicted)` or (only under `reject`, only when full) `refused(kept)`. @retention@ is the caller's cap: `evict`
keeps the newest @max@ and counts the oldest overflow into `dropped`, `reject` refuses past @max@ and evicts
nothing. NOT ATOMIC on its own — an append is a read-modify-write, so call it INSIDE a `store.exclusive` (or
a `serialize` domain), where it composes with the caller's own writes in one critical section; it opens no
domain of its own. T is the value's type and rides the STORE JSON boundary, so it carries `extends unknown`
for the same reason `exclusive_as` does: the value is stored as a public `unknown`, and a secret narrowed to
public would leak — the WRITE side is where that bound is load-bearing (the read side, `log_read`, needs
none).

`panic`. Only a `supervise` provider installed inside the program serves it: the runtime never machine-answers
`interrupted`, so signal it only below a provider.
declarations.name: interrupted

declarations.documentation:
Turn every `throw[T]` from the rest of the block into the supervision signal, carrying the thrown payload
UNCHANGED as the failure. The payload is already the program's own value, so nothing is wrapped and no

It converts TOTALLY, and that is not a limitation to work around — a throw handler must admit everything
the block can throw, so a converter that caught only part of `T` could not exist. Let the whole union
through and decide afterwards: `case my_fatal(...) -> prelude.throw(error = it)` in the `match` over the
signal is the same decision, written flat, where the reader can see it beside the other endings.

Written `use supervise.signal_throws[my_error]()`. It fixes the failure type to `T`, so it does not
stack with `signal_panics`; a block folding both channels writes one converter over the union it wants.

declarations.documentation:
Turn every panic from the rest of the block into the supervision signal, carrying `panicked(message)`.

A panic is the channel a runtime restart arrives on: an external call the runtime interrupted is never
re-run, and the frame that was holding it panics. That is the single most common failure a resident
meets, and folding it is why `once` exists — so this is the line that turns "the runtime restarted
under me" into a value the program can answer.

RETRYING a panic is an explicit choice, not a default: under `once` the interrupted call is not re-run
(right for an interrupted call, and required for a body that already had effects), while under `forever`
or `exponential` it is. The converter is the same either way; the mechanism below it decides.

Written `use supervise.signal_panics()`. It fixes the failure type to `panicked`, so it does not stack
with `signal_throws`; a block folding both channels writes one converter over the union it wants.
declarations.name: signal_panics

parameters.documentation: The rest of the block (bound by `use`).
parameters.label: continuation

declarations.documentation:
Run @task@ ONCE and answer with which happened — `ran(value)` or `signalled(failure)`. The other half of
this module: where `forever` and `exponential` answer an `interrupted` by RE-RUNNING the block, this one
answers it by handing the failure back as a value, and the task is never re-entered.

REACH FOR IT WHENEVER RE-RUNNING WOULD BE WRONG, which is more often than it looks. An external call the
runtime interrupted must NOT be re-run — the at-most-once rule is the runtime's, not a preference — so a
turn, a send or a question that died with the process wants to be REPORTED, not retried. A body that
already had effects before it failed must not repeat them, so "post the reply, then fail" retries into a
double post. And a failure that will answer the same next time is not a retry candidate at all, only a
fact to fold. In every one of those the question is what happened, and the answer is this sum.

THE SHAPE THIS REPLACES is a guard whose only job is to convert: `use handler { request panic(msg) {
break my_arm(msg) } }` (or the `prelude.throw` twin) wrapped around one call, with the success case
constructed by hand — which forces a named agent per call site, a data type per failure, and a sum
per site to name the pair. Here the converter still chooses `F`, so the failure keeps the caller's own
vocabulary; what goes away is minting `ok` / `failed` constructors again at every boundary.

@F@ is inferred from @task@ and preserved into `signalled`; `interrupted[F]` sits in @task@'s OVERWRITE
row because this agent DISCHARGES it. It catches ONLY the supervision signal — never `throw`, never `panic`,
which is the converter's business and stays visible in the source.
declarations.name: once

parameters.documentation: The work to run once, with `interrupted` served for it. A converter installed inside it (or around this call) decides which throws and panics become the signal.
parameters.label: task

declarations.signature: agent once[R, F, effect E](task: agent(value: null) -> R with {...E, interrupted[F]}) -> ran[R] | signalled[F] with E

declarations.documentation:
Replay the rest of the block on every `interrupted`, unbounded and with NO artificial delay: it re-runs at
once. The retry cadence is therefore set entirely by whatever the converter does BEFORE it signals — e.g. a
converter that performs a human-in-the-loop escalation and parks before signalling gives the attended /
re-auth loop, human-paced with no polling. Never re-raises and never returns on its own; a converter that
rethrows instead of signalling is how a failure leaves this loop. Written `use supervise.immediate()`.
declarations.name: immediate

parameters.documentation: The rest of the block (bound by `use`).
parameters.label: continuation

declarations.documentation:
Replay the rest of the block on every `interrupted`, unbounded, with exponential backoff capped at
@max_delay_milliseconds@. For daemons that must stay up across transient failures (e.g. keeping a
`time.watch` alive): it never re-raises and never returns on its own. The backoff delay lives in the loop's
own @delay@ var and grows by @factor@ per re-run up to the cap (`math.min`), so the durable state stays flat
across any number of replays. Written
`use supervise.forever(initial_delay_milliseconds = ..., factor = ..., max_delay_milliseconds = ...)`.
SUPERVISING A REGION: a converter cannot see a FIBER's failure. A fiber's panic is delivered to the region
as the typed `region.crashed` event rather than unwinding past `region.watch`, so a resident whose work runs
in fibers must perform `interrupted` from its `region.crashed` clause (installed inside this scope) — a
`panic` converter alone catches only the failures raised on the block's own path. What a re-run REBUILDS
is what the block installs: state a handler above this `use` owns survives every attempt, so install a desk
whose contents must outlive a reconnect above the scope, and whatever consumes that state on the same side
of the boundary.

parameters.label: factor

declarations.documentation:
Replay the rest of the block on `interrupted` with exponential backoff, up to @max_attempts@ times. On
failure number n (1-based) with n < @max_attempts@: durably sleep @initial_delay_milliseconds@ *
@factor@^(n-1), then re-run. When the budget is spent (the @max_attempts@-th `interrupted`): re-raise that
failure as a TYPED `throw[F]` — @F@ is the converter's chosen failure representation, so exhaustion keeps the
error typed end to end and never needs to re-panic. The attempt count and delay live in the loop's own vars
(one owner). The exhausted-vs-continue decision is genuine sum dispatch: the ONE comparison of the count to
the budget mints a `replay_after | give_up`, and the `signalled` arm `match`es it once — no code re-tests the
counter. Written `use supervise.exponential(initial_delay_milliseconds = ..., factor = ..., max_attempts = ...)`.

declarations.documentation:
Call @deliver_to@ once per @schedule@ occurrence, forever, passing the occurrence's scheduled epoch
millisecond as @time@. `watch` never resolves on its own (`-> never`); it runs until the run is
cancelled, at which point the in-flight delivery is cancelled and the watch tears down. @deliver_to@'s
effects @E@ flow to the caller's handlers unchanged.

Durability. The next occurrence is persisted; a restart re-arms it. If one or more occurrences were
missed while the runtime was down, `watch` fires EXACTLY ONCE immediately on recovery (the earliest
missed occurrence's scheduled time — it does not backfill every missed one), then continues on schedule.
Deliveries are serialized: the next occurrence is not armed until the current delivery settles, so a
@deliver_to@ slower than the interval simply rate-limits the ticks rather than queueing them.

No built-in retry. A @deliver_to@ that throws or panics is NOT retried — the failure propagates and kills
the watch, exactly as an uncaught failure in any callee does. Resilience is composed at the call site (a
`supervise` provider plus a converter around @deliver_to@), never baked into `watch`.
declarations.name: watch

parameters.documentation: When occurrences fire: an `interval(...)` or a `cron(...)` value.
parameters.label: schedule

parameters.documentation: Called once per occurrence; its @time@ is the occurrence's scheduled epoch millisecond, not the delivery instant.

and folded back by `from_civil`; a plain value carrying NO zone of its own — it means whatever offset
you read it at.
declarations.name: civil

parameters.documentation: The calendar year.
parameters.label: year

parameters.label: month

parameters.documentation: 1 to the month's length (`days_in_month`).
parameters.label: day

$katari_constructor.description: The tag that selects this variant. Write this exact string.

declarations.documentation:
Split an epoch-millisecond instant into its wall-clock fields at a fixed offset (@offset_minutes@
east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC). `from_civil` at the same offset is the exact inverse.

$katari_constructor.description: The tag that selects this variant. Write this exact string.

declarations.documentation:
Fold wall-clock fields back to an epoch-millisecond instant, reading them at a fixed offset
(@offset_minutes@ east of UTC; the default 0 means the fields are UTC). The exact inverse of
`to_civil` at the same offset. Out-of-range fields FOLD ARITHMETICALLY rather than erroring — month 13
is January of the next year, day 0 is the last day of the previous month, hour 24 is midnight of the
next day — so date arithmetic is plain field arithmetic: `day = value.day + 7` is one week later with
every carry handled.
declarations.name: from_civil

and folded back by `from_civil`; a plain value carrying NO zone of its own — it means whatever offset
you read it at.

first folds into its year like `from_civil` (month 13 is January of the next year).
declarations.name: days_in_month
declarations.signature: agent days_in_month(year: integer, month: integer) -> integer

declarations.documentation:
Format an instant as RFC3339 with millisecond precision — `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.mmmZ` at the default
UTC offset, the same wall clock with a `±HH:MM` suffix at a non-zero @offset_minutes@. The wire inverse
of `from_rfc3339`. A year outside 0..9999 renders faithfully (every digit, a leading `-`) even though
strict RFC3339 wants exactly four.
declarations.name: to_rfc3339
declarations.signature: agent to_rfc3339(epoch_milliseconds: number, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> string

declarations.documentation:
Parse an RFC3339 timestamp — `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS[.fraction]` followed by `Z` or `±HH:MM` — to an
epoch-millisecond UTC instant, or `null` when the string is not one (like `string.to_integer`).
Validated, not clamped: a month or day that does not exist (February 30th) is `null`, not a silently
carried date. `T` / `Z` also read lowercase; a fraction beyond milliseconds is truncated; a leap
second (`:60`) folds into the next minute.
declarations.name: from_rfc3339
declarations.signature: agent from_rfc3339(value: string) -> number | null

declarations.documentation:
The three-letter English label of an ISO weekday — 1 (Monday) through 7 (Sunday), the numbering
`day_of_week` answers. Anything outside 1..7 is `"???"`, so this is TOTAL: the parameter's type is
`integer` rather than a closed set, and a label that silently reads "Mon" for a bad index would hide
the arithmetic mistake that produced it.

A LABEL rather than the number, because "Sat" is what a model reads as a weekend without being told
the numbering, and a person reading a clock line does not want to count.
declarations.name: weekday_label

parameters.documentation: The ISO weekday, 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday); anything else answers "???".
parameters.label: day

day.description: The ISO weekday, 1 (Monday) to 7 (Sunday); anything else answers "???".

declarations.signature: agent weekday_label(day: integer) -> string

declarations.documentation:
An offset east of UTC as its `±HH:MM` label — the suffix that makes a rendered wall clock unambiguous,
so a model reading one can convert it against a timestamp it wrote itself. UTC renders `+00:00` rather
than `Z`: this is a label for a PERSON beside a civil time, where a sign lines up with every other row
and a lone letter does not. (`to_rfc3339`, which renders for the WIRE, spells UTC `Z` as RFC3339
requires — the two are different audiences, not an inconsistency.) A non-whole-hour offset renders
faithfully (Asia/Kathmandu's 345 is `+05:45`).
declarations.name: offset_label

parameters.documentation: The offset in minutes EAST of UTC — exactly what `zone_offset` answers.
parameters.label: offset_minutes

offset_minutes.description: The offset in minutes EAST of UTC — exactly what `zone_offset` answers.

declarations.signature: agent offset_label(offset_minutes: integer) -> string

declarations.documentation:
The instant's civil DATE at @offset_minutes@ (default UTC) as `YYYY-MM-DD` — the date half of
`to_rfc3339` without the clock, the zone or the `T`.

This is the shape to DATE things with, and the reason is ordering: ISO order is string order, so dates
in this form sort correctly with `array.sort`, compare with `<`, and group by prefix — a store key
`entries/2026-07-26` sits under `entries/2026-07` for free. A year outside 0..9999 renders every digit
(and a leading `-` for a negative one) rather than truncating, which loses the sort property but keeps
the date honest; the ordinary range is unaffected.
declarations.name: date_label

parameters.documentation: The instant, in epoch milliseconds.
parameters.label: epoch_milliseconds

parameters.documentation: The offset in minutes east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC.
parameters.label: offset_minutes

offset_minutes.description: The offset in minutes east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC.

declarations.signature: agent date_label(epoch_milliseconds: number, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> string

declarations.documentation:
The instant as a wall clock reads it at @offset_minutes@ (default UTC) —
`2026-07-26 (Sun) 14:32 +09:00`: the civil date, the weekday, the time to the minute, and the offset,
in one line.

The whole point is that a reader needs NO arithmetic. A model asked "how many days until the 31st" or
"is that this week" has the date AND the weekday in front of it, and a person handed the offset can
tell at a glance whether the clock is theirs. Seconds are deliberately absent: this is the line an app
injects into a turn or posts to an operator, where a second's precision is noise. Reach for
`to_rfc3339` when the reader is a machine.
declarations.name: stamp

parameters.documentation: The instant, in epoch milliseconds.
parameters.label: epoch_milliseconds

parameters.documentation: The offset in minutes east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC.
parameters.label: offset_minutes

offset_minutes.description: The offset in minutes east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC.

declarations.signature: agent stamp(epoch_milliseconds: number, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> string

declarations.documentation:
A civil DATE (`YYYY-MM-DD`) advanced by @days@ whole days at @offset_minutes@, answering a date in the
same shape — the arithmetic a recurring schedule needs ("the same weekday next week", "three days
before the due date"), without the caller touching a calendar. @days@ may be negative.

The date is read at NOON local, not midnight, and that is the load-bearing detail. A day is 86400000
milliseconds here, but a civil day at a zone's daylight-saving boundary is an hour longer or shorter;
anchored at midnight, adding whole days lands an hour either side of it and the render falls onto the
previous or next date — a weekly task quietly walking off its weekday, one hour at a time. Noon is
twelve hours from either edge, so the same arithmetic cannot cross a date boundary.

TOTAL: a @date@ that is not a `YYYY-MM-DD` civil date answers `null` rather than throwing — the string
is the whole explanation, so there is nothing a payload could add (the same reason `from_rfc3339`'s
failure is a `null`). Validated, not clamped: February 30th is `null`, not silently March 2nd.
declarations.name: add_days

parameters.documentation: The starting civil date, `YYYY-MM-DD` — exactly what `date_label` renders.
parameters.label: date

parameters.documentation: How many whole days to add; may be negative.
parameters.label: days

parameters.documentation: The offset in minutes east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC.
parameters.label: offset_minutes

date.description: The starting civil date, `YYYY-MM-DD` — exactly what `date_label` renders.

days.description: How many whole days to add; may be negative.

offset_minutes.description: The offset in minutes east of UTC; the default 0 reads UTC.

declarations.signature: agent add_days(date: string, days: integer, offset_minutes: integer ?= 0) -> string | null

declarations.documentation:
The offset of the IANA @zone@ in effect at @epoch_milliseconds@, in MINUTES EAST of UTC — exactly the
`offset_minutes` this module's agents take. Per-instant, so it is DST-correct by construction:
"America/New_York" answers -300 in January and -240 in July, and an instant one minute either side of
a transition gets the offset that was actually in force. "UTC" answers 0, and a zone whose offset is
not a whole hour answers it faithfully ("Asia/Kathmandu" is 345).

`null` when the runtime's zone database does not know @zone@ — a misspelling ("Asia/Tokio"), an
invented name, the empty string. The names it DOES know are exactly the ones a `cron` schedule's
timezone accepts, being the same database: canonical IANA names, their historical aliases ("Japan",
"Asia/Calcutta"), any letter case, and the legacy abbreviation spellings — but prefer a canonical
name, because an abbreviation names a whole zone WITH its DST rules rather than the standard offset it
looks like ("PST" answers -420 in July, not -480). The failure is a NULL rather than a throw for the
same reason `string.to_integer`'s is: the argument is the whole explanation, so there is nothing a
payload could add. Matching it is not optional, which is the point — a mistyped zone cannot silently
degrade to UTC and render wrong civil times.

Deterministic in its arguments: it reads no clock, so the answer for a given (@zone@,
@epoch_milliseconds@) never changes within a runtime and a replay recomputes the same offset. The only
drift possible is a zone database update between executions (a country changing its rules) — the same
drift a `cron` schedule already lives with. Pre-1900 instants, whose zones ran on local mean time
recorded to the second, round to the nearest minute.
declarations.name: zone_offset

parameters.documentation: The instant to read the offset AT, in epoch milliseconds; fractions floor, like `to_civil`.
parameters.label: epoch_milliseconds

parameters.documentation: An IANA zone name (e.g. "Asia/Tokyo", "America/New_York", "UTC"); an unknown name answers null.
parameters.label: zone

epoch_milliseconds.description: The instant to read the offset AT, in epoch milliseconds; fractions floor, like `to_civil`.

zone.description: An IANA zone name (e.g. "Asia/Tokyo", "America/New_York", "UTC"); an unknown name answers null.

declarations.signature: primitive agent zone_offset(epoch_milliseconds: number, zone: string) -> integer | null

declarations.documentation:
Serve a fresh, dynamically generated public webhook URL for the extent of @subscriber@. The
runtime converts every POST to the URL into a call of @callback@ (JSON body in, JSON result out,
validated against @callback@'s input schema). @subscriber@ receives the URL, registers it wherever
deliveries should come from, and stays alive while they flow; when it returns, the URL is
deactivated and its result becomes `inbound`'s result. Both callables' effects flow to the caller's
handlers unchanged.
declarations.name: inbound

parameters.documentation: Called once per POST. A body failing its input schema is rejected 400 before it runs; its unhandled failure cancels the endpoint.
parameters.label: callback

parameters.documentation: The URL's owner: receives the minted public URL, and the endpoint serves exactly while it runs.
parameters.label: subscriber

declarations.signature: external agent inbound[R, effect E](callback: agent never -> unknown with E, subscriber: agent(url: string) -> R with E) -> R with E | io from "webhook"
